records.value: The teacher leads a whole-class discussion anchored by the five area values now displayed on the demonstration table. Students are guided to say the pattern in words: the area of a slice is always the same fraction of the whole chapati's area as its central angle is of 360°. Students write this 'fraction rule' in their own words in their exercise books (for example, 'a 90° slice is 90/360 = 1/4 of the whole, so its area is 1/4 of the whole area'). Each student individually uses the rule on one new problem: 'A circular shamba (farm plot) in the Rift Valley has a radius of 20 metres. A farmer fences off a sector-shaped portion for planting maize, with a central angle of 72°. What is the area of the maize plot? Use π = 3.142.' Students find the fraction 72/360, find the area of the whole plot, then take that fraction of it, and self-check by comparing with a partner.

records.value: Strategy: DATA COLLECTION & PATTERN RECOGNITION. By physically measuring their own slice and computing its area using proportional reasoning ('what fraction of the whole is my slice?') — before any formula is named — students build the idea that a sector's area is the same fraction of the whole circle's area as its angle is of 360°. Seeing all five calculated areas displayed simultaneously on the demonstration table allows students to visually confirm the proportional relationship and check whether their prediction was correct. This 'discovery before definition' approach builds durable conceptual understanding; the formula itself is derived in Lesson 4.

records.value: Students individually draw an INITIAL MODEL in their exercise books. The prompt is: 'Draw a diagram that shows a circular pizza of radius r cut into a sector with central angle θ. Label all the parts you know. Write in words how you would find its area. Show using arrows or annotations WHY the rule makes sense — connect each part of the rule to a part of your diagram.' Students annotate their drawings with labels: centre of circle, radius r, central angle θ (in degrees), arc, sector. They write the area rule in words next to the sector (area of the slice = fraction of the circle × area of the whole circle) and add an annotation explaining each part (e.g., 'θ/360° = the fraction of the full circle that this slice represents'). These initial models are dated and will be revised in every subsequent lesson as understanding deepens.

records.value: Say: 'You now have the formula. Let's use it. I have three problems — each one connects the formula to a real situation in Kenya. Work in pairs. Show all working. You have 15 minutes.' Write the three problems on the board clearly, labelling θ and r for Problem 1 as a scaffold (θ = 80°, r = 15 cm). Do NOT scaffold θ and r for Problems 2 and 3 — learners must identify these from the problem text. Circulate actively. At the 5-minute mark, check that all pairs have completed Problem 1 correctly (A ≈ 157.1 cm²). For pairs still on Problem 1, ask: 'What is θ? What is r? Substitute.' For Problem 2, listen for confusion about 'pivot arm = radius'. If heard, ask the whole class: 'In the irrigation problem, what does the pivot arm represent geometrically?' — wait 10 seconds — cold-call 1 learner. At 15 minutes, say: 'Stop. Compare your answers with the pair next to you. You have 3 minutes to agree on a single set of answers.' After 3 minutes, cold-call one group of 4 to give each answer. Write the correct solutions on the board: P1 = 157.1 cm², P2 = 520 m² (nearest m²; 519.5 before rounding), P3 = 64π/5 cm² (exact, about 40.2 cm²). For Problem 3, say: 'Why did I ask for the answer in terms of π? Because it is EXACT. 64π/5 is more precise than any decimal. A craftsperson cutting beads to the millimetre would prefer this.' Connect back to the phenomenon: 'Every one of these problems is the same as our pizza slice — different radius, different angle, same formula.'

records.value: Distribute worksheets. Say: 'Use three different colours to shade the sector, the triangle, and the segment. You have 3 minutes — go.' Set a visible 3-minute timer. After colouring, cold-call 2 learners to name the area formula for the sector — they should say '(θ/360°)πr²' from Lesson 5. Then ask: 'What is the area of triangle OAB if OA = OB = r and the angle at O is θ?' Allow 15 seconds WAIT TIME. Cold-call 2 learners. Guide toward A = ½r²sinθ if not reached. Say: 'So if I take the sector and I remove the triangle, what am I left with?' Cold-call 1 learner. Then write the full derivation step by step on the board, pausing at each equals sign and asking the class to complete the next line chorally. For the watermelon worked example say: 'Substituting r = 14, θ = 60°: what is (60/360) × π × 14²? Calculate that now.' Allow 2 minutes of silent working. Cold-call 1 learner for the sector area value (~102.6 cm²). Then ask: 'First check that your calculator is in DEG (degree) mode — sin 60° must show 0.866, not −0.305. Now calculate ½ × 14² × sin60°. What do you get?' Cold-call 1 learner (~84.87 cm²). Finally: 'So the segment area is approximately…?' Cold-call 1 learner (~17.8 cm²: the unrounded value is 17.75 cm², and subtracting the rounded values 102.6 − 84.9 would give 17.7, so tell learners to keep the calculator values). Write the answer on the board next to the prediction wall estimates.

records.value: Learners independently complete the five-part summative task over approximately 14 minutes. The five parts are: Part A — calculate the arc length of the minor sector (answer: 29.32 m using the calculator π; 29.33 m using π = 22/7); Part B — calculate the area of the minor sector (answer: 307.88 square metres; 308.00 using π = 22/7); Part C — calculate the area of the major sector (answer: 1077.57 square metres; 1078.00 using π = 22/7; cross-checked as total circle area minus minor sector area); Part D — calculate the area of the minor segment (answer: minor sector area minus half times 21 squared times sin 80 degrees, giving approximately 307.88 minus 217.15 = 90.73 square metres); Part E — reflect: a farmer wants to plant maize on the minor segment only. Is this area enough to plant 200 maize plants if each plant needs 0.4 square metres? (Answer: 90.73 divided by 0.4 = 226.8, so yes, there is enough space.) After individual work, two learners present Parts C and D on the board, showing full working; the class checks Parts A, B and E against the answer key. The class listens, asks questions, and identifies any errors using the four-error checklist.

Guideline 12: the unit had no language support or access note. Added to the circle vocabulary review in Lesson 2 (where the circle terms first appear): English meaning plus sketch, a space for learners' home language, suggested Kiswahili terms, and an alternative way for learners with low vision or limited fine-motor control to take part. I am fairly confident of these Kiswahili terms (duara, kipenyo, nusu kipenyo, tao, mzingo, pembe, eneo) but they must be confirmed by a Kiswahili-speaking teacher before use. Teachers must decide the preferred Kiswahili wording; the 'sector' and 'segment' terms are deliberately left out because I cannot verify them.

LANGUAGE AND ACCESS SUPPORT: write each term on the board with a short English meaning and a sketch, and invite learners to say or write it in Kiswahili or their home language, for example duara (circle), kipenyo (diameter), nusu kipenyo (radius), tao (arc), mzingo (circumference), pembe (angle), eneo (area); teachers confirm the preferred Kiswahili terms. Give learners with low vision or limited fine-motor control the thick-card sectors to feel and a large-print diagram, and accept spoken or drawn explanations of the pattern as well as written ones.
